claim: The study recorded magnetoencephalographic (MEG) activity of participants who resolved XOR, OR, and AND functions as overt behavioral tasks with N = 10 participants per task.
source: we recorded the magnetoencephalographic (MEG) activity of participants who resolved the classic XOR, OR, and AND functions as overt behavioral tasks (N = 10 participants/task, N-of-1 replications)
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental design with specific sample sizes.

claim: Source-localized MEG activity progresses through four computational stages in each task.
source: In each task, we found that source-localized MEG activity progresses through four computational stages identified within individual participants
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The first computational stage involves initial contralateral representation of each visual input in occipital cortex.
source: (1) initial contralateral representation of each visual input in occipital cortex
evidence: This is described as one of the four identified computational stages from the MEG data.

claim: The second computational stage involves a joint linearly combined representation of both inputs in midline occipital cortex and right fusiform gyrus.
source: (2) a joint linearly combined representation of both inputs in midline occipital cortex and right fusiform gyrus
evidence: This is described as the second of four computational stages identified from MEG data.

claim: The third computational stage involves nonlinear task-dependent input integration in temporal-parietal cortex.
source: (3) nonlinear task-dependent input integration in temporal-parietal cortex
evidence: This is described as the third computational stage identified from MEG data.

claim: The fourth computational stage involves behavioral response representation in postcentral gyrus.
source: (4) behavioral response representation in postcentral gyrus
evidence: This is described as the fourth computational stage identified from MEG data.

claim: The spatiotemporal patterns of the first two computations are similar across the three tasks (XOR, AND, OR).
source: The spatiotemporal patterns of the first two computations are similar across the three tasks
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparing the computational stages across tasks.

claim: The last two computations are task specific.
source: the last two computations are task specific
evidence: This is stated as a finding distinguishing later computational stages from earlier ones.

claim: The primate visual system comprises the ventral and dorsal pathways with specific anatomical and functional hierarchical organization.
source: Extensive studies revealed that the primate visual system comprises the ventral and dorsal pathways, with specific anatomical and functional hierarchical organization (Van Essen et al., 1992; Kravitz et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Visual pathways compute over high-dimensional visual input starting with contralateral detection of simple, small features with small receptive fields.
source: These pathways compute over the high-dimensional visual input, starting separately in each hemisphere with contralateral detection of simple, small features with small receptive fields
evidence: This describes established knowledge about visual processing pathways.

claim: Simple features are hierarchically integrated into more complex, broader receptive field features in visual pathways.
source: that are then hierarchically integrated into more complex, broader receptive field features (Bugatus et al., 2017; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Kay et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on visual processing.

claim: Visual processing leads to integrated face, object, and scene features that are compared with memory to produce behavior.
source: leading to the integrated face, object, and scene features (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Sigala and Logothetis, 2002) that are compared with memory to produce behavior (Zhan et al., 2019b; Wyart et al., 2012; Ratcliff et al., 2009; Alamia and VanRullen, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The flow of information reverses when the same pathways predict the top-down input from memory.
source: This flow of information reverses when the same pathways predict the top-down input from memory (Friston, 2008; Linde-Domingo et al., 2019; Engel et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on predictive processing.

claim: XOR is a nonlinearly separable function.
source: XOR is famously a nonlinearly separable function
evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge about the XOR function.

claim: AND and OR are linearly separable functions.
source: whereas AND or OR is linearly separable
evidence: This is established mathematical knowledge about AND and OR functions.

claim: XOR, AND, and OR functions imply nonlinear vs. linear transformations of the same inputs in the considered architectures.
source: implying nonlinear vs. linear transformations of the same inputs in the considered architectures (Minsky and Papert, 2017; Rumelhart et al., 1986; Gidon et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on neural network architectures.

claim: The study recruited 35 participants, all right handed, with 24 women.
source: We recruited 35 participants (all right handed; 24 women)
evidence: This describes the participant sample in the methods section.

claim: All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision
evidence: This describes participant inclusion criteria.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee at the College of Medical, Veterinary and Life Sciences, University of Glasgow.
source: was approved by the ethics committee at the College of Medical, Veterinary and Life Sciences, University of Glasgow
evidence: This states the ethical approval for the study.

claim: An average face was synthesized using a generative photorealistic 3D face model.
source: We synthesized an average face using a generative photorealistic 3D face model (Yu et al., 2012; Zhan et al., 2019a)
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation method with citations.

claim: Black and clear lenses on glasses produced four different input conditions corresponding to four classes of logical inputs.
source: Black and clear lenses produced four different input conditions corresponding to four classes of logical inputs: (1) both clear, in vector notation [0,0], (2) left clear/right dark, [0,1]; (3) left dark/right clear [1,0]; and (4) both dark, [1,1]
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulus design.

claim: The edges of the left and right lens were 0.5 deg of visual angle away from the centrally presented fixation cross.
source: The edges of the left and the right lens were 0.5 deg of visual angle away from the centrally presented fixation cross
evidence: This specifies the spatial parameters of stimulus presentation.

claim: Each trial began with a central fixation cross displayed for a randomly chosen duration between 500 and 1000ms.
source: Each trial began with a central fixation cross displayed for a randomly chosen duration (between 500 and 1000ms)
evidence: This describes the trial structure in the experimental procedure.

claim: Stimuli were displayed for 150ms.
source: immediately followed by one of the four stimulus classes described above and displayed for 150ms
evidence: This specifies the stimulus presentation duration.

claim: Participants responded by pressing one of two keys with the index or middle fingers of their right hand.
source: to respond as quickly and accurately as possible by pressing one of two keys ascribed to each response choice with the index or middle fingers of their right hand
evidence: This describes the response method in the experimental procedure.

claim: Responses were 'same' vs. 'different' in the XOR task.
source: Responses were 'same' vs. 'different' in the XOR task
evidence: This specifies the response options for the XOR task.

claim: Responses were 'both dark' vs. 'otherwise' in the AND task.
source: 'both dark' vs. 'otherwise' in AND
evidence: This specifies the response options for the AND task.

claim: Responses were 'at least one dark' vs. 'otherwise' in the OR task.
source: or 'at least one dark' vs. 'otherwise' in OR
evidence: This specifies the response options for the OR task.

claim: Stimuli were presented in blocks of 80 trials.
source: Stimuli were presented in blocks of 80 trials
evidence: This describes the experimental block structure.

claim: Participants completed a total of 20–24 blocks split across 2–3 single day sessions.
source: Participants completed a total of 20–24 blocks split across 2–3 single day sessions
evidence: This describes the total experimental duration and structure.

claim: Each session lasted 2.5–3hr.
source: Each session lasted 2.5–3hr
evidence: This specifies the duration of each experimental session.

claim: MEG activity was recorded using a 248-magnetometer whole-head system at a 1017 Hz sampling rate.
source: We recorded the participants' MEG activity using a 248-magnetometer whole-head system (MAGNES 3600 WH, 4D Neuroimaing) at a 1017 Hz sampling rate
evidence: This describes the MEG recording equipment and parameters.

claim: Participants were excluded if the number of trials remaining after preprocessing was less than 700.
source: Participants were excluded if the number of trials remaining after preprocessing (eye movement artifact rejection and rejecting runs for excessive head motion) was less than 700
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Five participants were excluded resulting in a final sample size of N = 30 (10 per task).
source: We excluded five participants resulting in a final sample sizes of N = 30 (10 per task)
evidence: This reports the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: Mean head movement averaged across blocks across participants was 0.3 cm (min = 0.12, max = 0.44).
source: Mean head movement (averaged across blocks) across participants was 0.3 cm (min = 0.12, max = 0.44)
evidence: This reports a quality control metric for the MEG recordings.

claim: The median number of trials for subsequent analyses was 1064 (min = 701, max = 1361).
source: The median number of trials for subsequent analyses was 1064 (min = 701, max = 1361)
evidence: This reports the number of trials included in the analysis.

claim: Participants were accurate in all tasks with mean accuracy of 98.5% [97, 99] for XOR, 99% [98.6, 99.5] for AND, and 99.3% [99.2, 99.5] for OR.
source: Table 1 shows that participants were both accurate and fast in all tasks
evidence: Table 1 presents behavioral accuracy data for all three tasks.

claim: Median reaction times were 499ms [461, 557] for XOR, 457ms [393, 505] for AND, and 490ms [439, 541] for OR.
source: Table 1 shows that participants were both accurate and fast in all tasks
evidence: Table 1 presents reaction time data for all three tasks.

claim: There were no significant task differences on average accuracy and reaction times.
source: with no significant task differences on average accuracy and reaction times (RT), measured with independent sample t-tests
evidence: This reports the result of statistical comparisons between tasks.

claim: Linear representation of each input starts in contralateral occipital cortex around 60ms poststimulus.
source: The first computation linearly discriminates the 'on' vs. 'off' state of each input in contral-lateral occipital cortex ~60ms poststimulus
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about the timing and location of the first computational stage.

claim: Linear discrimination of both inputs occurs on occipital and ventral sources around 100ms.
source: This is followed by the linear discrimination of both inputs on occipital and ventral sources ~100ms
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about the timing and location of the second computational stage.

claim: Nonlinear integration of both inputs revealing the task solution occurs in parietal-temporal regions around 260ms.
source: followed by the nonlinear integration of both inputs, revealing the XOR, AND, or OR task solution in 2D source response space in the parietal-temporal regions ~260ms
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about the timing and location of the third computational stage.

claim: Nonlinear integration with RT-related activity occurs in postcentral gyrus around 400ms.
source: and finally the nonlinear integration with RT-related activity in postcentral gyrus ~400ms
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about the timing and location of the fourth computational stage.

claim: The four stages are common to XOR, AND, and OR, with the main task-related changes occurring in the latter two nonlinear stages.
source: These four stages are common to XOR, AND, and OR, with the main task-related changes occurring in the latter two nonlinear stages
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about similarities and differences across tasks.

claim: All statistical analyses were performed within each individual participant, controlling the familywise error rate over all considered sources and time points.
source: Notably, we performed all statistical analyses leading to these results within each individual participant, controlling the familywise error rate (FWER) over all considered sources and time points
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study.

claim: Each participant was treated as an N-of-1 study, with 10 participants per task providing 10 independent replications of the experiment.
source: By treating each participant as an N-of-1 study, 10 participants per task provide 10 independent replications of the experiment
evidence: This describes the replication approach used in the study design.

claim: The four computational stages were replicated in at least 9/10 participants.
source: We replicated the four computational stages in at least 9/10 participants (and in two further replication experiments with similarly high prevalence)
evidence: This reports the replication rate across participants.

claim: The Bayesian population prevalence of 9/10 replications is 0.89 [0.61 0.99].
source: Bayesian population prevalence (Ince et al., 2021) of 9/10 = 0.89 [0.61 0.99]
evidence: Table 2 provides the Bayesian population prevalence estimates.

claim: The Bayesian population prevalence of 10/10 replications is 1 [0.75 1].
evidence: Table 2 provides the Bayesian population prevalence estimates.

claim: Lin computation (left and right occipital sources) occurred in the time window 74–117ms and replicated in 10/10 participants for all three tasks.
source: Lin, left and right occipital sources [74–117ms]
evidence: Table 2 shows the replication of Lin computation across participants.

claim: LinBoth computation (occipital midline and right fusiform gyrus) occurred in the time window 74–117ms and replicated in 10/10 participants for all three tasks.
source: LinBoth, occipital midline and right fusiform gyrus [74–117ms]
evidence: Table 2 shows the replication of LinBoth computation across participants.

claim: NonLin computation in XOR occurred in parietal regions at 261–273ms and replicated in 9/10 participants.
source: NonLin, XOR: parietal [261–273ms]
evidence: Table 2 shows the replication of NonLin computation in XOR.

claim: NonLin computation in AND occurred in temporal-parietal regions at 246–304ms and replicated in 10/10 participants.
source: AND: temporal-parietal [246–304ms]
evidence: Table 2 shows the replication of NonLin computation in AND.

claim: NonLin computation in OR occurred in temporal-parietal regions at 261–304ms and replicated in 10/10 participants.
source: OR: temporal-parietal [261–304ms]
evidence: Table 2 shows the replication of NonLin computation in OR.

claim: RT-related computation in postcentral gyrus occurred at 386–398ms and replicated in 9/10 participants for XOR and AND, and 10/10 for OR.
source: RT, postcentral gyrus [386–398ms]
evidence: Table 2 shows the replication of RT-related computation across tasks.

claim: In right occipital source, the linear addition of vector responses [0,1] and [1,0] is close to the actual source response to [1,1].
source: The vector diagram (lower right quadrant) confirms that the linear addition of the vector responses [0, 1] and [1, 0] (gray point, sum of blue and red vector) is close to the actual source response to [1, 1] (black point)
evidence: This describes the linear nature of the computation in right occipital cortex based on vector analysis of MEG responses.

claim: In midline occipital LinBoth sources, all four stimuli are equally spread out in the quadrants of the source response space.
source: In midline occipital sources (Figure 3A,D), all four stimuli are equally spread out in the quadrants of the source response space (i.e. all inputs are equally discriminated)
evidence: This describes the pattern of responses in midline occipital sources as shown in Figure 3.

claim: In right fusiform gyrus LinBoth source, the [1,0] and [0,1] stimuli are discriminated with opposite activity, whereas [1,1] and [0,0] stimuli are less discriminated.
source: In contrast, the right fusiform gyrus source (Figure 3A,E) discriminates the [1,0] and [0,1] stimuli with an opposite activity, whereas the [1,1] (black dot) and [0,0] (gray dot) stimuli are less discriminated
evidence: This describes the pattern of responses in right fusiform gyrus as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The right fusiform gyrus LinBoth stage likely represents an important intermediate step toward the computation of XOR.
source: So, the right fusiform gyrus LinBoth stage likely represents an important intermediate step toward the computation of XOR
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed response patterns in right fusiform gyrus.

claim: In parietal NonLin source for XOR, responses to [1,0] and [0,1] stimuli are magnetic fields with the same dipole orientation.
source: In parietal source NonLin, responses to [1,0] and [0,1] stimuli are magnetic fields with the same dipole orientation, suggesting that the same pattern of cortical activity (i.e. the same neural population) responds to both stimuli
evidence: This describes the MEG response pattern in parietal cortex and infers the underlying neural population activity.

claim: In right fusiform gyrus LinBoth source, responses to [1,0] and [0,1] are magnetic fields with different dipole directions, suggesting different neural populations respond to each stimulus.
source: In right fusiform gyrus source LinBoth (Figure 3A, E), responses to [1,0] and [0,1] are magnetic fields with different dipole directions, suggesting that different neural populations within the region modeled by the source respond to each stimulus
evidence: This describes the MEG response pattern and infers the underlying neural population activity.

claim: In parietal NonLin source for XOR, the representation of [1,1] is nonlinear, pointing away from the sum of the individual input responses.
source: Second, the representation of [1,1] (black dot) is now nonlinear (green vector), pointing away from the sum of the red and blue vectors of the individual inputs
evidence: This describes the nonlinear nature of the computation based on vector analysis of MEG responses.

claim: Following nonlinear transformation in parietal cortex, the XOR outputs are linearly decodable in the 2D MEG response space.
source: Following this nonlinear transformation, the XOR outputs are now linearly decodable in the 2D MEG response space
evidence: This describes the consequence of the nonlinear transformation for task output representation.

claim: Postcentral gyrus source activity relates trial by trial to behavioral reaction times.
source: In addition, this source activity now relates trial by trial to behavioral RTs
evidence: This describes the relationship between MEG activity and behavior in the fourth computational stage.

claim: Stage 4 postcentral gyrus and frontal regions source activity primarily relates to behavioral reaction times.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows that this last postcentral gyrus fourth stage (also in frontal regions) primarily relates to behavioral RTs
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the relationship between source activity and RT.

claim: In AND task, the task output is linearly separable in the 2D MEG response space with the [1,1] response further from other stimulus classes.
source: In AND, the task output is linearly separable in the 2D MEG response space: the black [1,1] response is further from the other stimulus classes than they are from each other
evidence: This describes the pattern of responses in AND task NonLin stage.

claim: In OR task, the task outputs are linearly separable with the [0,0] stimulus class represented apart from the other ones.
source: In OR, the task outputs are also linearly separable, with the gray [0,0] stimulus class represented apart from the other ones
evidence: This describes the pattern of responses in OR task NonLin stage.

claim: Later post-200ms computational stages involve nonlinear task-specific stimulus representations in ventral and parietal areas.
source: This shows how these later post-200ms computational stages involve nonlinear task-specific stimulus representations in ventral (NonLin) and parietal (NonLin, NonLin&RT) areas
evidence: This summarizes the findings about later computational stages across tasks.

claim: The systems-level approach aims to reverse engineer the hierarchy of brain computations that represent and transform sensory inputs to produce behavior.
source: Our systems-level approach aims to reverse engineer, from mass brain signals, the hierarchy of brain computations that represent and transform sensory inputs to produce behavior—i.e., the brain's algorithm of the behavioral task
evidence: This describes the conceptual framework and goal of the study.

claim: The four stages of computation meet the five key properties of an algorithm: specified inputs, specified outputs, definite sequence, effectiveness in the brain, and finite processing time.
source: The four stages of computation that we systematically found in each individual participant and tasks meet the five key properties of an algorithm: (1) the inputs were specified as the four possible combinations of two binary inputs; (2) the output responses were also specified as the responses of the logical functions XOR, OR, and AND; (3) the algorithms were definite in each task, with a sequence of two characterized Lin and two NonLin computations that transformed the same inputs into the task-specific outputs; the algorithms were also (4) effective in the brain, in the sense that they only relied on brain resources, and (5) finite in processing time, producing behavior with ~450–500ms
evidence: This argues that the identified computational stages constitute an algorithm based on formal properties.

claim: Reverse engineering a systems-level algorithm at the granularity of MEG brain measures does not preclude the existence of different compositions of algorithms at lower levels of granularity.
source: Note that reverse engineering a systems-level algorithm at the granularity of MEG brain measures does not preclude the existence of different compositions of algorithms at lower levels of granularity of individual neurons that together implement the higher-level algorithm (much like the lower granularity algorithms of machine language implement the higher-level algorithms of C++)
evidence: This discusses the relationship between different levels of algorithmic description.

claim: Systems-level analysis provides constraints on where and when specific computations take place, enabling targeted studies across modalities and granularities of brain measures.
source: Rather, such systems-level analysis provides constraints on where (the brain regions) and when (the specific time windows) specific computations take place, enabling targeted studies of the algorithmic 'how' across modalities and granularities of brain measures
evidence: This discusses the utility of the systems-level approach for future research.

claim: A key challenge in generalizing to naturalistic categorization tasks is that task-relevant features may be completely different for different behaviors and participants.
source: A key challenge is that the task-relevant features of real-world faces, objects, and scenes, may be completely different for different behaviors and participants, effectively changing the inputs to the algorithm
evidence: This discusses challenges in extending the approach to more complex tasks.

claim: Task- or participant-specific features are generally not considered in studies of neural representation, processing, and categorization.
source: Unfortunately, task- or participant-specific features are generally not considered in studies of neural representation, processing, and categorization
evidence: This critiques current approaches in the field.

claim: Understanding task- or participant-specific features remains a challenge for deep convolutional neural network research.
source: Their understanding remains a similar challenge for deep convolutional neural network research, including instances when these are used as models of the brain
evidence: This discusses limitations of current computational models.

claim: Different modalities or granularities of brain measures will likely provide complementary understandings of computations in different brain regions.
source: Different modalities or granularities of brain measures (e.g. M/EEG, 3/7T fMRI, NIRS vs. single electrodes (Gidon et al., 2020) and electrode arrays) will likely provide complementary understandings (e.g. timing vs. location) of the computations in different brain regions
evidence: This speculates about future research directions using different measurement techniques.

claim: Data-driven clustering analysis delivered four stages of computation in the XOR, AND, and OR tasks.
source: First, we performed a data-driven clustering analysis that delivered four stages of computation in the XOR, AND, and OR tasks (see Methods, Clustering the Stages of Computation and Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used to identify computational stages.

claim: K-means clustering with k = 5 was selected as a good solution for XOR, AND, and OR tasks.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows that the XOR, AND, and OR tasks all had k = 5 as a good solution
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows the results of k-means clustering analysis.

claim: The five clusters include a stage 0 before any computation starts, and then four distinct timed stages with different brain volumes of computations.
source: First, a stage 0, before any computation starts, and then four distinct timed stages with different brain volumes of LinLeft, LinRight, LinBoth, XOR, AND, and OR computations
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: Stage 1 (LinLeft and LinRight) and stage 2 (LinBoth) are similar across all tasks.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B reveals that stage 1 (LinLeft and LinRight, cyan and orange) and stage 2 (LinBoth, magenta) are similar across all tasks
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows the similarity analysis across tasks.

claim: Stages 3 and 4 (NonLin and NonLin & RT) are specific to each task.
source: whereas stages 3 and 4 (i.e. NonLin, green; NonLin & RT, yellow) are specific to each task
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows the task-specificity of later stages.

claim: The first two linear stages of XOR with Gabor stimuli generalize to the first two linear stages of XOR, AND, and OR with face stimuli.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows, for each Gabor participant, that their first two linear stages do indeed generalize to the first two linear stages of XOR, AND, and OR faces
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows the generalization analysis between stimulus types.

claim: The third and fourth NonLinear stages of XOR with Gabor stimuli only generalize to the third and fourth stages of XOR with face stimuli.
source: whereas their third and fourth NonLinear stages only generalize to the third and fourth stages of XOR faces
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows the task-specific generalization of later stages.

claim: Three participants resolved XOR with Gabor stimuli showing similar stages of computation as with face stimuli.
source: we demonstrate the generalization of the three participants (P1, P2, P3) who resolved XOR with Gabor stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows the replication with Gabor stimuli.

claim: In the sequential presentation experiment, linear representation of the first input started around 80ms poststimulus with a peak around 100ms.
source: Linear representation of the first input started around 80ms poststimulus (with a ~100ms peak; or around –900ms with respect to second lens presentation)
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows the results of the sequential presentation experiment.

claim: In the sequential presentation experiment, the second input was linearly represented from around 100ms with a peak at around 120ms.
source: The second input was linearly represented from ~100ms with a peak at ~120ms (blue, orange, and magenta time courses)
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows the timing of second input representation.

claim: The sequential presentation experiment replicated the results of the simultaneous presentation experiment.
source: Averaged time courses of the Lin and NonLin computations across individual participants (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2) replicated the results of Figure 1
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows the replication of computational stages with sequential presentation.

claim: Multivariate R² was used to quantify the fit of linear models in the 2D response space of each source.
source: We quantified the fit in the 2D response space of the source with a multivariate R2 that quantifies multivariate variance as the determinant of the covariance matrix
evidence: This describes the statistical metric used to assess linear model fit.

claim: A log-likelihood ratio test was used to determine whether the nonlinear interaction term significantly improved model fit.
source: A log-likelihood ratio (LLR) tested whether the added interaction term significantly improved model fit (p<0.05), FDR corrected over time points and sources (Groppe et al., 2011; Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001)
evidence: This describes the statistical test used to assess nonlinear representations with citations.

claim: Pairwise Mahalanobis distances were computed between the 2D distributions of single trial MEG activity in response to each input class.
source: First, we computed the pairwise Mahalanobis distances as detailed below between the color-coded 2D distributions of single trial MEG activity in response to each input class (see Figure 3)
evidence: This describes the distance metric used to characterize representation patterns.

claim: Gaussian-Copula mutual information was used to quantify the association between reaction times and MEG activity.
source: We used information theory to quantify the association between RTs and MEG activity, as MI (<RT; MEGt>), splitting RTs into four equiprobable bins and using continuous MEG (on all sources and time points). To this end, we used Gaussian-Copula mutual information Ince et al., 2017 on all sources and time points
evidence: This describes the information theoretic method used to relate MEG activity to behavior with citation.

claim: Source reconstruction was performed using a Linearly Constrained Minimum Variance beamformer with parameters 'lambda = 6%' and 'fixedori = no'.
source: We computed the Linearly Constrained Minimum Variance beamformer (Hillebrand and Barnes, 2005) solution with parameters 'lambda = 6%' and 'fixedori = no'
evidence: This describes the source reconstruction method with specific parameters and citation.

claim: Statistical analyses were performed on 5107 cortical grid points after excluding cerebellar and noncortical sources.
source: Using a Talairaih-Daemon atlas, we excluded all cerebellar and noncortical sources and performed the statistical analyses on the remaining 5107 cortical grid points
evidence: This describes the spatial extent of the statistical analysis.

claim: Nonparametric statistical thresholds were computed using the method of maximum statistics to control familywise error rate.
source: To control the FWER over all considered time points and sources, we computed a nonparametric statistical threshold with the method of maximum statistics (Groppe et al., 2011)
evidence: This describes the multiple comparisons correction method with citation.
